name: ADA4522-2ARZ-R7
title: ADA4522-1/-2/-4: 55 V zero-drift, low-noise, rail-to-rail output op amps with input EMI filters
summary: Single, dual and quad chopper-stabilised operational amplifiers for supplies of 4.5 V to 55 V (±2.25 V to ±27.5 V). Offset is 5 µV maximum at 5 V and 30 V with drift of 22 nV/°C maximum (dual, 30 V), voltage noise 5.8 nV/√Hz with chopping that suppresses 1/f noise, and 117 nV p-p from 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz. The input range includes the negative rail, the output swings rail to rail, gain-bandwidth is 2.7 MHz, and each input carries an RF filter and clamp. Specified from −40 °C to +125 °C; the ADA4522-2ARZ-R7 is the dual in 8-lead SOIC.

circuits.title: Discrete 3-op-amp instrumentation amplifier (Figure 82)
circuits.description: Two amplifiers buffer the inputs and set the first-stage gain with RG1, RG2, R1 and R3; the third amplifier with R2, R4, R5 and R6 takes the difference and refers it to ground. Output = (VIN2 − VIN1)(1 + R1/RG1)(R5/R2). Common-mode rejection rests on R5/R2 = R6/R4.
notes: Values from the Table 10 example, with RG1 = RG2, R1 = R3, R2 = R4 and R5 = R6.
The amplifiers run from a single supply with V− at ground.
A 1 % ratio match limits common-mode rejection to 34 dB; resistors of 0.01 % or better are called for.

circuits.title: Precision weigh scale measurement system (Figure 83)
circuits.description: A six-wire load cell feeds the two halves of an ADA4522-2 wired as the input stage of a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with gain 1 + 2R1/RG. C1 and C2 across the feedback resistors low-pass filter the signal; R3, R4, C3, C4 and C5 filter common-mode and differential noise ahead of the AD7791 sigma-delta converter. The load cell's sense lines drive the converter's reference inputs, so the reading is ratiometric to the excitation.

parts.note: six-wire bridge: excitation, ground, two sense, two output

notes: Board copper adds error: a 1 oz trace 0.005 inch wide and 1 inch long measures roughly 100 mΩ at room temperature, so 10 mA through it drops 1 mV; the separate sense lines take the bridge voltage at the cell.

circuits.title: Low-side current sensing circuit (Figure 84)
circuits.description: A 0.1 Ω shunt in the ground return of the load is read by one amplifier as a difference amplifier with gain R2/R1 = 1000, so VOUT = 1000 × RS × I = 100 × I (volts per ampere). The system's common-mode rejection is set by the resistor match R1/R2 = R3/R4.
notes: At 1 A the shunt drops 100 mV; at 1 mA it drops 100 µV, which calls for very low offset and drift.

circuits.title: Stability compensation with isolating resistor RISO (Figure 80)
circuits.description: A unity-gain buffer driving a capacitive load CL through a series resistor RISO; feedback is taken from the amplifier pin, ahead of RISO, so the load capacitance is isolated from the loop. Overshoot against CL for RISO = 0 Ω, 25 Ω and 50 Ω is in Figure 81.

parts.note: isolating resistor; 25 Ω and 50 Ω in Figure 81

notes: RISO raises the output impedance seen by the load and lowers gain accuracy.

circuits.title: Unity-gain follower with feedback resistor RF for large source resistance (Figure 89)
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower fed through source resistance RS, with RF from the output to the inverting input. With a large RS and a slowly rising supply the output can rail to the positive supply; choosing RS and RF per Table 11 prevents it.

circuits.title: Circuit for large signal transient response (Figure 75)
circuits.description: Unity-gain buffer with 100 Ω in series with each input, loaded by 100 pF and 10 kΩ, driven by a 50 V p-p step; the circuit behind Figure 74.

circuits.title: Comparator configuration A (Figure 86)
circuits.description: The amplifier run open loop as a comparator: the inverting input pulled to +VSY and the noninverting input to −VSY, each through 10 kΩ, with ammeters A1 and A2 reading ISY+ and ISY− in the supply leads (Figure 88).

circuits.title: Comparator configuration B (Figure 87)
circuits.description: The opposite input polarity to configuration A: the noninverting input pulled to +VSY and the inverting input to −VSY, each through 10 kΩ, with ammeters in both supply leads.

operation.text: ADA4522-1, ADA4522-2 and ADA4522-4 hold one, two and four amplifiers. The single and dual come in 8-lead MSOP and 8-lead SOIC, the quad in 14-lead TSSOP and 14-lead SOIC. All are specified at 5 V, 30 V and 55 V supplies over −40 °C to +125 °C.
Operates from 4.5 V to 55 V on one supply, or ±2.25 V to ±27.5 V split. The absolute limit across the supply pins is 60 V.

The input common-mode range reaches the negative rail and stops 1.5 V short of the positive rail (0 V to 3.5 V on 5 V, to 28.5 V on 30 V, to 53.5 V on 55 V). The output swings rail to rail. Driven beyond the input range as a ±15 V buffer, the output clips on the high side but does not reverse phase (Figure 73).

Three gain stages (Gm1, Gm2, Gm3) with internal compensation capacitors. Input and output chopping switches run at 4.8 MHz and move the input stage's offset and 1/f noise up to that frequency; an offset and ripple correction loop clocked at 800 kHz, the amplifier's switching frequency, suppresses the resulting artifacts. Chopping also corrects offset changes with common-mode voltage and supply, giving 160 dB typical CMRR and PSRR at 30 V. Each channel has its own thermal shutdown.

Each input passes through 200 Ω (RS1, RS2) into a filter of two common-mode capacitors and one differential capacitor, with −3 dB points of 50 MHz common mode and 33 MHz differential. ESD diodes D1 to D4 run from the inputs to both rails and stay reverse biased in normal use; inputs survive about 300 mV beyond either rail. After the filter, the antiparallel diodes D5 and D6, about 1 V forward drop each, guard the input stage against large differential transients.
The differential input is rated ±5 V. Beyond that, more than ±10 mA flows through D5 or D6, which shortens the part's life and can destroy it.

If an input can go more than 300 mV past a rail, the ESD diodes conduct; add a series resistor at each input to hold the current to ±10 mA. The resistor adds thermal noise: at ±15 V the amplifier's broadband noise is about 5.8 nV/√Hz at unity gain, a 1 kΩ resistor adds 4 nV/√Hz, and the sum is about 7 nV/√Hz.

Keep the junction below 150 °C; the shutdown does not guarantee survival above that. Each channel shuts off when its junction reaches 190 °C: its output goes high impedance and its quiescent current falls to 0.1 mA. It turns back on at 160 °C. A sustained overload, such as excessive output current, makes the channel cycle between the two temperatures.
Bring both supplies up together. Where that cannot be done, the positive supply comes up before the negative supply.

In unity gain with a fast input step, D5 and D6 conduct and the output edge has two parts: a quick jump, then a slew at the specified slew rate (Figure 74). With a low source resistance (100 Ω in Figure 75) or a large step, the output current is capped at the short-circuit current, and the input-to-output difference is set by that current times the total input resistance plus the diode drop. With a high source resistance or a small step, the current is the step divided by the source resistance. A larger resistor in series with the noninverting input lowers the input current; a resistor in the feedback path lowers the output current. Closed-loop gain stages, with their smaller inputs and gain resistors, rarely see this.
Chopping greatly reduces 1/f noise, so noise at dc and low frequency is far lower than in conventional low-noise amplifiers; 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz noise is 117 nV p-p (Figure 64).

With source resistance below 1 kΩ the amplifier's voltage noise dominates; as it rises the resistor's thermal noise takes over, and above about 50 kΩ the current noise term leads. The amplifier is meant for low source resistance: at about 6 nV/√Hz, adding 1 kΩ at the input raises total noise to 7.2 nV/√Hz.

Above the flat region the noise spectrum shows a broad bump centred at 6 MHz from the falling input-stage gain, a narrow peak at the 4.8 MHz chopping frequency, and a bump at 800 kHz from the correction loop with a peak whose size varies between units; some units show peaks at multiples of 800 kHz such as 1.6 MHz and 2.4 MHz, others none. Where the closed-loop bandwidth reaches past these frequencies, run higher gain or filter the output. In Figure 77 the 800 kHz peak is about 38 nV/√Hz unfiltered, 4.1 nV/√Hz with an 80 kHz post filter, and below the noise floor with an 8 kHz filter.

Current noise density at unity gain is about 1.3 pA/√Hz at 1 kHz (Figure 78). It is measured as voltage noise across a 100 kΩ source resistor, which with the input and board capacitance rolls the measurement off well below the amplifier's bandwidth.

Out-of-band RF picked up on any pin can be rectified by the input devices and appear as a dc offset. The integrated input filters give the noninverting input an EMIRR of 72 dB at 400 MHz rising to 85 dB at 2400 MHz (100 mV peak).

Loads up to 250 pF are stable in any configuration. Above 250 pF use external compensation, most of all at unity gain, the worst case; a series resistor RISO between output and load (circuit riso) is one way, at the cost of higher output impedance and lower gain accuracy.
Wire any unused amplifier as a unity-gain buffer with its input held at mid-supply.

In the discrete instrumentation amplifier the first stage runs at high gain, so A1 and A2 need low offset and low noise; the difference stage runs at low gain and matters less for noise. Keep RG1 and RG2 small, since their thermal noise is multiplied by the full noise gain (Table 10).

Keep the board clean and dry to avoid leakage. Place bypass capacitors as close to the supply pins as possible and keep supply traces short. Route signal traces 5 mm or more away from supply lines. Thermocouple voltages arise where solder meets traces and component leads when the two ends of a part sit at different temperatures: orient resistors so heat reaches both ends equally, give both input paths the same number and kind of junctions (a zero-ohm resistor can balance a real one), place matched parts close and alike, use equal lead lengths, keep heat sources away from the inputs, and use a ground plane to spread heat and reduce pickup.

Not recommended. D5 and D6 are substrate PNP transistors that conduct once the differential input passes about 600 mV, and they then carry current to the lower rail, raising total supply current. Both test configurations (circuits comparator-a and comparator-b) give the same result: at 30 V, ISY+ stays at 1.55 mA per dual amplifier while ISY− rises to nearly 2 mA (Figure 88), with 10 kΩ at each input; smaller input resistors raise the current further.

operation.topic: Large source resistance in a follower
operation.text: As a unity-gain follower with a large source resistance and a slowly ramping supply, the output can rail to the positive supply. Lower RS or add a feedback resistor RF as Table 11 sets out (circuit follower-rf).
